entries.clue: Setter left offensive musical (9)

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as ME

annotation.surface: A cranky setter walks out of a West End show they found distasteful.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like a noun, the show being walked out of, but it is the adjective the answer means. 'Setter' for ME is a crossword habit: the compiler speaking of themself.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tune that is pleasant to hear can be called either word.

entries.clue: Signifies a way to an end (5)

blocks.note: the verb: what a word or sign indicates
the noun, from the idiom about a route to a goal

annotation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss on how a thing indicates its purpose.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition leans on the idiom 'a means to an end', so the phrase nearly hands you the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: the verb for what a word signifies, and the noun in the idiom about reaching an end.

entries.clue: Criminal nearly admitting constant theft (7)

indicators.note: a criminal version of the letters is a corrupted one
letting C in, as a door admits a visitor

blocks.note: c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

annotation.surface: Someone who has almost owned up to a string of thefts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' reads as 'almost', trimming a word; here it is simply the six letters to rearrange, with nothing removed.
annotation.definitionFit: The legal name for the offence rather than a casual synonym; English law used it until 1968.

entries.clue: Stray diamonds found by fissure (5)

blocks.note: D for diamonds, the card suit
a rift is a crack or split

annotation.surface: Loose diamonds turning up beside a crack in the rock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stray' reads as an adjective describing the diamonds; it is the verb, to wander off.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: a boat or a mind that wanders off course is said to do both.

entries.clue: Manage to put poem in Old English (7)

indicators.note: together with 'in': place one thing inside another
'in' means inside, so with 'to put' it sets the poem inside the abbreviation

annotation.surface: A struggling scholar managing to write a poem in the language of Beowulf.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Manage to' looks like the start of an instruction; only 'Manage' is the definition, and 'to put ... in' is the container.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the workplace: supervising a project is running it.

entries.clue: Radiance of old prunes misrepresented (9)

indicators.note: presented wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

annotation.surface: An advert that oversold how glowing some elderly dried plums were.
annotation.walkthrough: Old prunes are the least radiant thing imaginable, which is the joke of the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Close synonyms for dazzling brightness, and both extend to grandeur.

entries.clue: Embrace European giant (4)

annotation.surface: A welcoming hug for a very tall visitor from the Continent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Giant' is the adjective here, as in a giant leap, not the fairy-tale noun the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective sense of 'giant', as in a giant leap: very big.

entries.clue: Bad actor rejected food somewhere in Germany (7)

indicators.note: sent back, so GRUB turns round

blocks.note: a ham is an overacting performer

annotation.surface: A poor actor on tour in Germany sending his dinner back.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface invites a burger joke, but the answer is the port city itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the northern port is one place in Germany among many.

entries.clue: Eager aunt breaking promise (9)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

annotation.surface: A keen aunt going back on her word.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' belongs with 'promise' on the surface; in the cryptic reading it acts on the two words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the answer being the more formal and binding word.

entries.clue: Hot ether limit is fine (8)

blocks.note: H for hot, as on a tap
the ether is the upper air
a line is a boundary or limit

annotation.surface: A lab note that some warm ether is within the permitted limit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as 'acceptable'; it means very thin.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective sense of 'fine' meaning very thin, as in a crack no wider than a hair.

entries.clue: Move clumsily having taken drug for a spinal region (6)

definitions.note: LUMBAR is an adjective, 'of the lower back'; the clue gives the region it describes

indicators.note: the word takes on a new letter
A stands in place of the drug

blocks.note: to lumber is to move heavily and clumsily
used literally, going in where the E was

annotation.surface: Someone staggering about after taking something for their back pain.
annotation.walkthrough: The drug here is E for ecstasy, and it is the letter swapped out of LUMBER, not something added to it.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective names the lower part of the spine, so the clue gives the region it describes.

entries.clue: Climb like US currency (6)

blocks.note: as = like, in the manner of
the cent, a hundredth of a dollar

annotation.surface: A rising dollar, read as a financial headline.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Climb' could be verb or noun; the answer needs the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun sense of 'climb': the act of going up a slope.

entries.clue: Remarkable urinals distributed around gents initially (8)

indicators.note: the letters are spread out and rearranged
the rearranged letters sit either side of G
take the first letter of 'gents'

annotation.surface: A remarkable arrangement of urinals in a gents' lavatory.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'gents' is a British men's public toilet, which is why the urinals are there.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Remarkable' in the sense of one of a kind, as in a talent unlike any other.

entries.clue: Start to cover artificial fabric in marker (6)

indicators.note: the start of 'cover', its first letter

annotation.surface: Upholstering something in synthetic cloth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Start to cover' reads as a phrase about beginning a job; here it takes just one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a waxy coloured stick is one kind of marker.

entries.clue: Fight back as consumer holds dog upside down (9)

indicators.note: the consumer holds the dog inside it
in a down clue, the whole assembly is read bottom to top

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow, or tail, them

annotation.surface: A diner grappling with an inverted dog, which then fights back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is the verb, to follow closely, not an animal; 'upside down' flips the whole assembled word, not just the dog.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for striking back at someone who struck first.

entries.clue: Nearly behind revolting lines at the end of the day (9)

indicators.note: turning over, so AFT comes out backwards

annotation.surface: Protest lines left behind as evening comes on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' reads as disgusting or rebellious; it is the reversal instruction for 'behind' only.
annotation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: the coming of darkness is how the day closes.

entries.clue: Stretch out scandal involving owner of X? (8)

indicators.note: the scandal involves, or takes in, the name

blocks.note: Elon Musk owns X, formerly Twitter
-gate is the suffix for a scandal, after Watergate

annotation.surface: A scandal engulfing the billionaire behind X.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Involving' usually wraps one thing round another, but here the scandal simply takes the name at its front; the question mark flags a topical figure.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for making something longer.

entries.clue: Direct view across revolutionary paintings (8)

indicators.note: the view stretches across the paintings, holding them
turning round, so ART becomes TRA

annotation.surface: A gallery-goer looking past some radical canvases.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests radical art; it only turns the paintings round.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Direct' as in a route with no bends.

entries.clue: In the morning I get fit and friendly (7)

annotation.surface: A morning person feeling healthy and sociable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get' reads as part of the wordplay, but it only joins the pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for good-natured and easy to get on with.

entries.clue: Dish boxed up by souvenir retailer (7)

indicators.note: the answer is boxed inside the words that follow
in a down clue, read the letters upwards

annotation.surface: A plate packed up for a tourist by a gift-shop keeper.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a souvenir plate being boxed for the journey, so 'Dish' feels like part of the story rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The word names both the earthenware pot and the pâté cooked in it, so either reading makes it a dish.

entries.clue: Wearing a wig is tough (6)

blocks.note: a rug is slang for a wig, so this is a jokey 'fitted with a rug'
hardy, able to withstand rough treatment

annotation.surface: A claim that wearing a hairpiece takes nerve.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense is playful: RUG is slang for a toupee, so someone wearing one has been 'rugged'.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Tough' as in hardy and craggy; the wig sense is a jokey coinage from slang for a toupee.

entries.clue: Animal rebuilt log lair (7)

indicators.note: the letters are pulled apart and put together again

annotation.surface: A creature reconstructing its den from timber.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface gives an animal building a den, which fits a great ape's nightly nest-making.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the largest ape is one animal among many.

entries.clue: Head of church to dawdle around section in monastery (8)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
'around' means encircling, so dawdling wraps round the S

annotation.surface: A church leader lingering in part of a monastery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Section in monastery' reads as one phrase naming a part of the building, but 'section' is only a letter and the definition is 'monastery'.
annotation.definitionFit: The word for a covered walkway extends to the whole religious house, a place of seclusion.

entries.clue: Extend feast (6)

blocks.note: to stretch or open out further
a lavish meal laid out on a table

annotation.surface: An invitation to make the banquet last longer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feast' is the noun: a generous meal laid out on the table.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb means to stretch out, and the noun is a lavish meal laid out for guests.

entries.clue: Rigid back (5)

blocks.note: the back of a ship, not of a person

annotation.surface: A stiff back, the kind bad posture gives you.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as the body part; it is the rear of a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective is strict and unbending; the noun is the rear of a ship.

entries.clue: Strength shown by idiot alien (5)

annotation.surface: A foolish extraterrestrial displaying unexpected muscle.
annotation.walkthrough: ET is the standard crossword alien, from the Spielberg film.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of a good quality that counts in your favour.

entries.clue: Meat father gives character from Greece (6)

annotation.surface: A dad serving roast lamb to a Greek visitor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person in a story; here it means a letter of the alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Greek L is one character of that alphabet.

entries.clue: One portion is minute showing impracticality (8)

blocks.note: a deal is a share or portion, as in a great deal

annotation.surface: Complaining that a single tiny serving is unrealistic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as the adjective, tiny; it is the unit of time.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose fit: pursuing ideals over realities is, to a critic, impracticality.

entries.clue: Pure and simple pool (4)

blocks.note: nothing more than, as in 'only a child'
a small lake, as in the lake name Windermere

annotation.surface: A plain, clean pond.
annotation.walkthrough: The water sense is mostly British, surviving in lake names in the English Lake District.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective means nothing more than; the noun is a small lake, mostly British.

entries.clue: Revolting alien wit I prepare to ambush (3,2,4)

indicators.note: rising up and overturning, so the letters get thrown about

annotation.surface: A disgusting extraterrestrial comedian plotting an ambush.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolting alien' is a B-movie monster on the surface; 'Revolting' is only the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase describes hiding in readiness, which is exactly how an ambush is prepared.
